title: Error Recognition
text:
Textile practices such as crochet and knitting have recently experienced a widespread resurgence. Many creative activities traditionally rooted in manual craftsmanship, once considered less relevant in the context of industrialization and globalization, are now being rediscovered. Skills that historically required years of hands-on experience can, however, be difficult and discouraging for beginners, especially for adults who approach these practices with limited time, resources, or access to expert guidance. Crochet is a notable example: although widely practiced across cultures and historically spread in Europe through Italian convents in the sixteenth century, it remains technically demanding and highly dependent on the maker’s ability to recognize and correct errors. The COVID-19 pandemic further contributed to this renewed interest, encouraging many people to explore slow, creative, and tactile activities.


Despite this revival, crochet performed using mechanical devices has seen relatively little technological development. Existing crochet machines remain strongly operator-dependent and offer limited support for automated quality monitoring. Moreover, hobbyist tools such as circular crochet looms, widely available and inexpensive, provide no error feedback and require constant attention from the user. In this work, we start from a commercially available circular loom intended for hobby use and, through a series of mechanical, electronic, and software modifications, transform it into a fully automated crochet machine capable of self-monitoring. This approach demonstrates how accessible off-the-shelf tools can be augmented and repurposed into automated systems, lowering the barrier to entry for creative technologies.



A single undetected defect, such as missing yarn, incomplete engagement, or a misaligned loop, may propagate across many subsequent cycles, compromising the entire production and resulting in wasted time and materials. For hobbyists and individual makers, this leads to frustration and loss of work. For small and medium-sized factories, the consequences extend to production inefficiencies and environmental impact. As the textile industry is one of the major contributors to global waste and pollution, improving error detection and reducing material waste is a relevant challenge from both practical and sustainability perspectives.



Automating the early detection of such defects requires monitoring the hook at the precise moment when the yarn configuration becomes informative. In the scenario addressed in this work, a correctly formed stitch appears as a characteristic “U”-shaped engagement around the base of the hook. Any deviation from this expected pattern must be identified promptly to prevent the defect from propagating downstream.



In this section, we present a lightweight, real-time embedded vision system for hook-level error detection implemented entirely on a Raspberry Pi 3 equipped with a CSI camera module and mounted on a custom 3D-printed support.
A hardware microswitch mounted on the machine provides a synchronization signal marking the exact phase of the hook movement, enabling image acquisition at each cycle for real-time inspection.
In this way system captures images in synchrony with the machine’s motion, isolates the region of interest, and analyzes it using a dedicated detection algorithm capable of distinguishing correct yarn engagement from error conditions.
Our goal is to support both individual makers, who may not have access to industrial-grade equipment, and future industrial applications, where inline quality monitoring could significantly reduce waste and promote more sustainable textile manufacturing.

The acquisition system plays a central role in the proposed error detection pipeline, as it must provide close-up images of the hook region at every relevant movement of the crochet machine.
In this work, we start from a commercially available circular crochet loom intended for hobby use and adapt it into an automated system through a set of mechanical and electronic modifications.
This choice allows us to preserve the low-cost and accessible nature of the original tool while enabling precise synchronization and repeatable inspection of each hook.



Overview of the circular crochet loom.
Source: Sentro Official Website.


A hardware microswitch mounted on the modified loom generates a synchronization signal that marks the exact moment in the hook’s motion when the yarn configuration becomes informative.
This signal is used by the Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to trigger image acquisition in real time.
At each trigger, the system inspects the hook to verify that the yarn—regardless of its color, thickness, or texture—assumes the expected “U”-shaped configuration around the base of the hook.
Any configuration that does not match this pattern is classified as an error.
When an anomaly is detected, the system immediately stops the motor driving the process and displays a diagnostic message indicating the index of the affected hook.
An example close-up of the inspected region is reported in these two figures.





Examples of correct and defective yarn configuration.









The primary objective of the acquisition system is to enable automatic, hook-level monitoring of the knitting process on a low-cost embedded platform.
To meet this goal, the choice of camera and interface must satisfy the following requirements:

Compatibility with Raspberry Pi 3: use of natively supported interfaces and libraries.
Ease of software integration: availability of well-established computer vision libraries (e.g., libcamera, Picamera2, OpenCV).
Cost-effectiveness: sufficient resolution to distinguish fine yarn details while keeping costs low.
Close-focus capability: ability to capture sharp images at short distances near the hook area.
Low power consumption: efficient power usage to minimize the overall system load.

These requirements guided the evaluation of several acquisition architectures for the Raspberry Pi 3, considering their impact on image quality, latency, software complexity, and mechanical integration.






The Raspberry Pi Camera v2.1 connects directly to the Broadcom SoC through the MIPI–CSI interface, a high-speed differential serial bus dedicated to video capture.
This direct link offers several advantages for the considered application:

High bandwidth and low latency: the pixel stream reaches the processor without traversing the USB or network stack, resulting in reduced jitter and more deterministic timing.
Image quality and control: the 8 MP sensor, combined with the Raspberry platform’s integrated image signal processor (ISP), provides fine control over exposure, gain, white balance, and frame rate.
Native integration: the camera is supported via libcamera / Picamera2 and V4L2, with stable pipelines toward OpenCV, TensorFlow Lite, and other vision frameworks.

In the context of hook-level defect detection, these properties translate into a favorable signal-to-noise ratio and consistent frame characteristics, which are beneficial for detecting subtle differences in yarn configuration.
The low and predictable latency also facilitates accurate synchronization between the microswitch event and the captured image, which is critical for reliable inspection.




The ESP32-CAM module integrates an OV2640 sensor (2 MP) and a microcontroller with on-board Wi-Fi connectivity.
In a typical setup, images are captured on the ESP32-CAM and transmitted to the Raspberry Pi for processing, either via Wi-Fi or over a serial link:

Wi-Fi: the module sends JPEG or MJPEG frames to a broker or server.
Wiring is simple, but latency and jitter depend on network conditions, buffering, and retransmissions.
Serial / USB–UART: the module transmits image data in chunks to the Raspberry Pi through a UART–USB bridge.
This reduces dependence on the wireless network, but requires application-level protocols for fragmentation, reassembly, and buffering.

The ESP32-CAM is extremely low cost and can operate as a stand-alone node.
However, compared to a CSI-connected Pi Camera, it provides lower image quality and less precise control over acquisition parameters.
On-board compression may obscure fine textile defects, and the less deterministic timing makes it harder to align the acquisition instant with the hook motion.
From a mechanical standpoint, the ESP32-CAM module is also bulkier than the Pi Camera, complicating its integration into the compact 3D-printed frame of the desktop crochet machine.
On the positive side, its shorter minimum focus distance can be advantageous for very close-up shots, potentially reducing the need for additional optics.



In preliminary experiments with a direct USB–UART connection, the ESP32-CAM was successfully flashed with a MicroPython firmware.
However, upon reboot, the board remained stuck in the bootloader, and the serial output consisted only of unreadable characters or repetitive error messages, never reaching a stable REPL prompt.
This behavior prevented the validation of a reliable point-to-point communication channel with the Raspberry Pi and hindered further development of the serial-based approach.




A Wi-Fi-based architecture was also evaluated, in which the ESP32-CAM periodically captured JPEG snapshots and published them to an MQTT topic, while the Raspberry Pi—running a Mosquitto broker—subscribed to the topic, decoded the images, and displayed or stored them locally.
Despite its conceptual simplicity, this approach suffered from practical issues related to the transmission and reconstruction of the JPEG payloads.
Decoding errors and corrupted frames frequently occurred, making it impossible to guarantee consistent image delivery for real-time detection.
Given these early difficulties and following an iterative, prototype-driven development process, the ESP32-CAM solutions were deemed insufficiently reliable for the timing and robustness requirements of hook-level error detection, and effort was redirected toward more tightly integrated alternatives.







Standard USB webcams offer a ready-to-use and widely available solution, typically with UVC support under Linux.
However, image data must traverse the USB stack, introducing additional overhead compared to CSI and limiting the level of low-level camera control.
Such devices are suitable for early prototyping or applications with less stringent latency requirements, but are less attractive when deterministic timing and compact integration are needed.



The Raspberry Pi HQ Camera is a 12 MP module with a C/CS mount for interchangeable lenses.
It provides superior optical quality and flexibility in terms of focus, focal length, and macro optics, at the cost of higher price and significantly larger size compared to the Pi Camera v2.1.
The HQ Camera is therefore more appropriate when extreme close-ups or professional optical control are required, whereas the present work prioritizes low cost and compactness.






Considering the functional requirements, the practical experiments with the ESP32-CAM, and the constraints of the crochet machine, the Pi Camera v2.1 connected via the MIPI–CSI interface emerged as the most suitable option.
It combines sufficient resolution and close-focus capability with low and deterministic latency, strong software support on the Raspberry Pi 3, and a compact form factor compatible with the 3D-printed camera mount described in Section @sec:camera_mount.
This configuration is therefore adopted as the reference acquisition system for the error detection pipeline.

This behavior prevented the validation of a reliable point-to-point communication channel with the Raspberry Pi and hindered further development of the serial-based approach.




A Wi-Fi-based architecture was also evaluated, in which the ESP32-CAM periodically captured JPEG snapshots and published them to an MQTT topic, while the Raspberry Pi—running a Mosquitto broker—subscribed to the topic, decoded the images, and displayed or stored them locally.
Despite its conceptual simplicity, this approach suffered from practical issues related to the transmission and reconstruction of the JPEG payloads.
Decoding errors and corrupted frames frequently occurred, making it impossible to guarantee consistent image delivery for real-time detection.
Given these early difficulties and following an iterative, prototype-driven development process, the ESP32-CAM solutions were deemed insufficiently reliable for the timing and robustness requirements of hook-level error detection, and effort was redirected toward more tightly integrated alternatives.







Standard USB webcams offer a ready-to-use and widely available solution, typically with UVC support under Linux.
However, image data must traverse the USB stack, introducing additional overhead compared to CSI and limiting the level of low-level camera control.
Such devices are suitable for early prototyping or applications with less stringent latency requirements, but are less attractive when deterministic timing and compact integration are needed.



The Raspberry Pi HQ Camera is a 12 MP module with a C/CS mount for interchangeable lenses.
It provides superior optical quality and flexibility in terms of focus, focal length, and macro optics, at the cost of higher price and significantly larger size compared to the Pi Camera v2.1.
The HQ Camera is therefore more appropriate when extreme close-ups or professional optical control are required, whereas the present work prioritizes low cost and compactness.






Considering the functional requirements, the practical experiments with the ESP32-CAM, and the constraints of the crochet machine, the Pi Camera v2.1 connected via the MIPI–CSI interface emerged as the most suitable option.
It combines sufficient resolution and close-focus capability with low and deterministic latency, strong software support on the Raspberry Pi 3, and a compact form factor compatible with the 3D-printed camera mount described in Section @sec:camera_mount.
This configuration is therefore adopted as the reference acquisition system for the error detection pipeline.

title: Display Interface and Three-Colour Servo Control
text:
The current prototype integrates the operator interface, pattern loading and three-colour yarn actuation in a single control workflow.
A Pimoroni GFX HAT is mounted on the Raspberry Pi and acts as the local human-machine interface (HMI). Through its LCD display and capacitive touch buttons, the user can:

browse the .png patterns stored on a USB flash drive;
select the pattern to be manufactured;
start, pause and resume the process;
monitor the completion percentage;
receive status or alarm messages.

The real-control application is implemented in:
gfxhat_pattern_ui_usb.py
Unlike the initial display-only prototype, the current script is directly connected to the ESP32 through a USB serial connection. The Raspberry Pi interprets the selected pattern and sends the required colour command, while the ESP32 drives the three servomotors and reads the synchronization microswitch.

Current implementation status. Pattern selection, display interaction, USB communication with the ESP32, microswitch synchronization and three-servo actuation are implemented. The camera-based error-recognition output and the automatic yarn-cut notification screen are already supported by the interface, but are not yet connected to the physical process in the present test setup.





The control system is divided into a high-level Raspberry Pi layer and a low-level ESP32 actuation layer.
Personal computer
└── Pattern Editor
    └── .png patterns saved on USB flash drive

Automated knitting machine
├── Raspberry Pi
│   ├── Pimoroni GFX HAT display and touch interface
│   ├── USB flash drive pattern loading
│   ├── PNG validation and pixel-to-colour conversion
│   ├── Progress visualization
│   └── USB serial communication with ESP32
│
└── ESP32
    ├── Servo 1: colour-selection actuator 1
    ├── Servo 2: colour-selection actuator 2
    ├── Servo 3: colour-selection actuator 3
    ├── 3D-designed servo arms
    └── Synchronization microswitch
The communication between the Raspberry Pi and the ESP32 no longer uses the Raspberry Pi UART header pins. The ESP32 is connected to the Raspberry Pi through its USB cable, which provides:

power supply for the ESP32 board;
USB-to-serial communication between Raspberry Pi and ESP32.

The servomotors are powered separately by an external regulated 5 V DC-DC supply.




The Pimoroni GFX HAT combines:

a 128 × 64 monochrome LCD;
six capacitive touch buttons;
RGB backlighting;
six indicator LEDs associated with the touch buttons.

In this project it is used as an embedded user interface mounted directly on the Raspberry Pi. The screen provides immediate information about the current process state, while the touch buttons allow the user to operate the machine without an external keyboard or monitor.
The interface is controlled by the GfxScreen and PatternApp classes in gfxhat_pattern_ui_usb.py.


The application implements the following states:







State
Purpose




SELECT_FILE
Lists the PNG patterns found on the USB drive


INSERT_YARNS
Confirms the selected pattern and asks the user to prepare the yarns


RUNNING
Shows pattern progress during the real manufacturing sequence


STOPPED
Pauses the actuation while preserving the current position in the pattern


ALERT
Displays an error or manual-intervention message


DONE
Indicates that the selected pattern has been completed

Function

Select previous PNG file


DOWN
Select next PNG file


SELECT
Confirm the selected file


PLUS
Refresh file list / start / resume


MINUS
Pause the current process


BACK
Return to the pattern-selection menu



When the application is executed in demo mode, BACK and SELECT can also be used to simulate the alert screens without actuating the motors.





The complete real-operation sequence is:
Insert USB flash drive containing PNG patterns
        ↓
Power on Raspberry Pi, ESP32 and servo power supply
        ↓
Launch gfxhat_pattern_ui_usb.py
        ↓
Select a PNG file from the GFX HAT screen
        ↓
Selected PNG is copied locally on the Raspberry Pi
        ↓
Display shows: "INSERIRE I FILATI"
        ↓
User presses PLUS / AVVIA
        ↓
Raspberry Pi validates the PNG and opens the USB serial connection
        ↓
The first colour-selection servo command is sent to the ESP32
        ↓
Each microswitch press produces a NEXT message
        ↓
Raspberry Pi advances to the next pixel and updates the progress bar
        ↓
At the end of the pattern, all servos are moved to their DOWN position
        ↓
Display shows: "LAVORO COMPLETATO"
When a PNG file is selected, the script copies it from the USB drive to a local working file:
~/automated_knitting_machine/patterns/current_pattern.png
This prevents removal of the USB flash drive from interrupting a process after the pattern has already been selected.




The selected image is validated before actuation begins.

Required value

.png

Exactly 48 pixels

Exactly 3 distinct RGB colours


File location on USB drive
Directly in the mounted USB root directory



The image height determines the total number of processed rows, while the total number of actuator updates corresponds to:
total pixels = width × height



The three RGB colours are automatically associated with the three servo commands in order of first appearance while scanning the image:

The pixels are read sequentially from the image. For each current pixel, only the servo associated with the corresponding colour is moved to its active position, while the other two servos remain in their inactive position.

Before starting the physical process, the operator must verify that the real yarn colours placed on the three servo mechanisms correspond to the automatically generated RGB-to-servo mapping printed in the terminal.






The colour-selection subsystem consists of three servomotors, each associated with one yarn or colour channel.

C2


Servo 3

For each pixel, the ESP32 receives one colour command and sets the actuator positions so that one channel is active at a time:
C1 → Servo 1 UP, Servo 2 DOWN, Servo 3 DOWN
C2 → Servo 1 DOWN, Servo 2 UP, Servo 3 DOWN
C3 → Servo 1 DOWN, Servo 2 DOWN, Servo 3 UP
DOWN → all servos DOWN

These angles are calibration values and must be adjusted according to the final mounting position, servo horn orientation, printed arm geometry and the required yarn displacement.




To mechanically transfer servo rotation to the yarn-selection elements, three dedicated arms were designed in 3D and mounted on the servomotors.
The purpose of the designed components is to:

provide a repeatable connection between each servo shaft and the moving selection element;
convert the servo angular rotation into the required mechanical displacement;
keep the three yarn channels geometrically consistent;
allow the angular limits to be calibrated without modifying the electronic architecture;
make the mechanical components easy to reproduce through 3D printing.



Each printed arm must be mounted on its corresponding servo horn and oriented consistently before the firmware limits are calibrated.
A recommended assembly procedure is:

keep the printed arm disconnected from the yarn-guiding mechanism;
power the servo electronics and send the DOWN command;
mount the arm in the intended inactive orientation;
send the corresponding active command (C1, C2 or C3);
verify that the motion is unobstructed and reaches the desired displacement;
adjust UP_n and DOWN_n in the ESP32 firmware if necessary;
repeat the procedure for all three actuators before attaching yarns.




The CAD model and exported printing files can be stored in a dedicated mechanical folder, for example:
mechanics/
└── servo_arms/
    ├── servo_arm_source_file
    ├── servo_arm_left.stl
    ├── servo_arm_centre.stl
    ├── servo_arm_right.stl
    └── assembly_render.png
Suggested images to include in this documentation page are:

a CAD render of the three designed arms;
a printed arm mounted on one servomotor;
a photograph of the complete three-servo selection module;
a detail view showing the active and inactive positions.


Mechanical safety note. The first powered tests should be performed without yarn tension and without obstructing the printed arms. If a servo stalls against a mechanical stop, disconnect the actuator supply and recalibrate the angles before continuing.






The ESP32 firmware is implemented in:
servo_switch_usb.ino
The ESP32 is responsible for:

generating the servo commands through the ESP32Servo library;
reading the microswitch;
debouncing the microswitch signal;
receiving actuation commands from the Raspberry Pi;
notifying the Raspberry Pi when the next synchronized control instant occurs.



The microswitch has three terminals: COM, NO and NC. Only COM and NO are used.



Microswitch terminal
ESP32 connection




COM
GND


NO
GPIO25

Not connected



The firmware configures the input as:
pinMode(pinMicroswitch, INPUT_PULLUP);
Therefore:



Microswitch state
GPIO25 value
Meaning




Not pressed
HIGH
No advancement event


Pressed
LOW
Send NEXT to Raspberry Pi



A software debounce interval of 50 ms is applied so that one physical press generates only one valid advancement message.



Arduino compiles all .ino files inside the same sketch folder together. For this reason, the new firmware must be kept in its own sketch directory:

├── uart_switch_3servo_png/
│   └── uart_switch_3servo_png.ino
│
└── servo_switch_usb/
    └── servo_switch_usb.ino
Only servo_switch_usb/servo_switch_usb.ino must be opened and uploaded for the USB-controlled prototype.





The Raspberry Pi and ESP32 communicate over the USB cable connected to the ESP32 micro-USB port.
In the tested configuration, the ESP32 is enumerated by the Raspberry Pi as:
/dev/ttyUSB0
The communication baud rate is:
115200 baud
The value must be identical in the two programs:
# Raspberry Pi: gfxhat_pattern_ui_usb.py
BAUD_RATE = 115200
// ESP32: servo_switch_usb.ino
Serial.begin(115200);

When the user presses AVVIA, the Raspberry Pi immediately sends the colour command corresponding to the first pixel. After that:

the current colour is physically selected by the servo mechanism;
a machine cycle reaches the synchronization point;
the microswitch is pressed;
the ESP32 sends NEXT;
the Raspberry Pi marks the current pixel as completed;
the progress bar is updated;

At the last valid NEXT, the application completes the progress counter, sends the servos to DOWN during controller shutdown and shows the completion screen.

sudo raspi-config

Interface Options

AttributeError: module 'gfxhat.lcd' has no attribute 'contrast'

python3 -m serial.tools.list_ports -v

the three servos are powered by the external 5 V supply;
the external supply ground is connected to ESP32 ground;
the printed servo arms can move freely;
the microswitch is wired to COM and NO;
the selected PNG is 48 pixels wide and contains exactly three colours.






The integrated Raspberry Pi application is organized into four main parts.


Handles:

LCD rendering;
RGB backlight configuration;
active touch-button LEDs;
progress bar display;
screen cleanup on application exit.




Handles:

state transitions of the user interface;
USB pattern discovery and selection;
local pattern copy;
touch-button events;
screen rendering;
progress and alert events.




Handles the real machine control logic:

PNG validation;
RGB-to-servo command mapping;
USB serial port opening;
serial message exchange with the ESP32;
progress advancement after each NEXT;
servo deactivation on pause, completion or shutdown.

The serial reading loop runs in a separate worker thread. This prevents the graphical interface from freezing while it waits for a physical microswitch event.



Simulates progress without using the ESP32 or actuators and is used to verify the interface before hardware tests.





When the operator presses MINUS during operation:

the interface enters the STOPPED state;
the Raspberry Pi sends DOWN to the ESP32;
all three printed servo arms return to the inactive position;
the current pixel index is preserved;
any NEXT event generated while paused is ignored.

When the operator presses PLUS to resume:

the application returns to the RUNNING state;
the command corresponding to the current pixel is sent again;
processing continues from the preserved pattern position.


The current pause function controls the three colour-selection servo mechanisms. If a separate main machine motor is introduced, its stop and resume commands must be added to the ESP32 firmware and to the serial protocol.







Before attaching yarns or applying mechanical load:

upload servo_switch_usb.ino to the ESP32;
connect the ESP32 to the Raspberry Pi through USB;
connect the three servos to the ESP32 signal pins and to the external 5 V supply;
connect all grounds;
mount the 3D-printed arms without forcing them against the structure;
start a simple three-colour PNG pattern;
observe the UP and DOWN positions of each arm;
adjust the angle constants in the ESP32 firmware where necessary:

The image acquisition and error-recognition pipeline is implemented in Python and runs directly on the Raspberry Pi 3.
The system operates in a fully event-driven manner: each activation of the microswitch triggers an image capture, an immediate crop of the region of interest (ROI), and a real-time evaluation of the yarn configuration using a log-likelihood ratio (LLR) classifier.



To train and evaluate the classifier, a dedicated dataset of cropped hook images was collected directly from the machine.
At present, the dataset includes three yarn colors:

light blue
purple
fuchsia

Although these colors appear visually quite different in RGB, their behavior after preprocessing (grayscale conversion, CLAHE enhancement, ROI masking) is not uniform.
Preliminary qualitative inspection suggested that the fuchsia yarn could be challenging due to its visual similarity to the pink background of the machine.
However, subsequent experiments revealed that raw chromatic contrast is not the primary factor affecting detectability in the proposed NCC–LLR pipeline.
After grayscale conversion, the light blue yarn becomes closer in intensity to the machine background, resulting in lower separability between correct and defective configurations.
Conversely, the fuchsia yarn exhibits stronger and more consistent local texture variations within the discriminative ROI, which makes the LLR scores for (H_0) and (H_1) more distinct despite its low RGB contrast.
The purple yarn displays intermediate behavior, with moderate grayscale separability.
To further probe the limits of the method, additional experiments were conducted using a pale pink yarn whose color is almost indistinguishable from the background.
Under this condition, neither the NCC-based similarity nor the CLAHE-enhanced preprocessing provided sufficient discriminative information for reliable classification, and the LLR method consistently failed to separate the two hypotheses.
This extreme low-contrast scenario is therefore considered out of scope for the current handcrafted method and highlights the need for future solutions based on learned or color-invariant features.


 Light blue

 Purple

 Fuchsia




 Pale pink (failure)


Figure: Examples of yarn colors used in the dataset.
The pale pink yarn is almost indistinguishable from the machine background and cannot be reliably detected by the current method.




Upon a rising edge from the microswitch (handled via the gpiozero library), the software captures a still image using the Picamera 2.1 interface.
Since only a small portion of the full frame contains the hook region, the image is immediately cropped according to a predefined ROI, specified either in relative coordinates or in absolute pixel values.
This cropping stage reduces computational cost and increases robustness by ensuring that the classifier operates on a stable and consistent portion of the scene.
Boundary checks are applied to avoid invalid crops in case of slight camera misalignment, which is important due to the sub-centimeter positioning precision required for hook-level inspection.




The LLR classifier relies on two prototype images:

a positive prototype representing correct yarn engagement;
a negative prototype representing a hook that has failed to catch the yarn.

These prototypes are computed as the median of small training sets of positive and negative examples.
Before prototype computation, images undergo grayscale conversion, Gaussian denoising, and light contrast equalization using CLAHE, improving robustness to illumination variability and sensor noise.




The LLR classifier does not operate on the entire cropped image, but only within a discriminative region of interest (ROI).
This ROI is defined by a soft mask computed offline using a separate Python script (build_mean_diff_mask.py), which analyzes pre-cropped patches of both positive and negative examples.
The script takes as input two sets of images: a positive set (--pos) and a negative set (--neg).
All images are converted to grayscale, denoised, equalized with CLAHE, and resized to a common resolution of (76 ) pixels.
For each pixel location, the script computes a Fisher-like separability score:
\[
S(i,j) \propto
\frac{|\mu_{\text{pos}}(i,j) - \mu_{\text{neg}}(i,j)|}
{\sigma_{\text{pos}}(i,j) + \sigma_{\text{neg}}(i,j) + \varepsilon}
\]
The resulting score map is normalized to ([0,1]) and restricted to a fixed rectangular zone corresponding to the physical region where the yarn intersects the hook.
Outside this area, the mask is set to zero so that the LLR classifier ignores those pixels.
To preserve local texture, the soft score map (S) is optionally smoothed with a bilateral filter.
A global threshold is then selected using Otsu’s method, producing a hard binary mask.
The script saves: - the soft mask (mask_soft.png) - the hard mask (mask_hard_otsu.png) - a visualization of the rectangular ROI
At runtime, the soft mask is used as a per-pixel weighting function in the NCC computation:
\[
s_{\text{pos}} = \text{NCC}(I, \mu_{\text{pos}}; \text{mask}), \qquad
s_{\text{neg}} = \text{NCC}(I, \mu_{\text{neg}}; \text{mask})
\]
Among the available yarn colors, the fuchsia yarn was specifically included to demonstrate that the proposed method does not rely on RGB contrast.
Despite its visual similarity to the background, the preprocessing pipeline enables reliable detection.


 mask_soft.png

 mask_hard_otsu.png


Figure: Visualization of the ROI masks used during computation.




For each cropped image, the classifier computes two normalized cross-correlation (NCC) scores:
\[
s_{\text{pos}}, \quad s_{\text{neg}}
\]
The decision variable is defined as:
\[
LLR = s_{\text{pos}} - s_{\text{neg}}
\]
A threshold on the LLR score is selected to minimize false negatives, which are more detrimental than false positives in this application.
If the threshold is not satisfied, the hook is classified as defective and an immediate stop command is issued.




The complete implementation—including synchronized image capture, ROI extraction, preprocessing, prototype generation, and real-time LLR evaluation—is available at:
https://github.com/AlessiaRinaldi/error_recognition_knitting_machine

Mechanical support, 3D printing, working distance, and CAD notes.

The camera mounting solution combines a commercially available __magnetic-base stand_ with a custom 3D-printed support designed specifically for the Raspberry Pi Camera module.
The magnetic base provides a rigid and highly stable foundation, while allowing fine manual adjustment in height, angle, and lateral position through its articulated arm.


A custom holder for the Raspberry Pi Camera v2.1 was designed in Autodesk Fusion 360 and fabricated using fused deposition modeling (FDM) with PLA filament on a Bambu Lab A1 Mini 3D printer.
The printed part encloses the camera PCB and incorporates a series of mounting holes and a pin that fits into the threaded end of the magnetic base arm.



While the magnetic stand and the 3D-printed camera holder provide sufficient stability for prototyping, the overall stiffness of the structure is not optimal yet.
Small shifts caused by machine vibration or accidental contact can slightly alter the camera pose over time, affecting the exact position of the region of interest in the image.

The performance of the proposed LLR-based detector was evaluated within the binary hypothesis-testing framework:

\]
and compares it to a fixed threshold to decide between (H_0) and (H_1).

section: Threshold Selection with the Validation Set
text:
Threshold Selection with the Validation Set
With the initial threshold (LLR = 0), at least one false alarm occurred. Since a false alarm would unnecessarily stop the real machine, the threshold was adjusted following a Neyman–Pearson criterion, prioritizing a false-alarm rate as close as possible to zero.
The selected threshold was:
\[
LLR_{\text{thr}} = -0.035
\]
This threshold was then kept fixed during the final independent test.

text:
Out-of-Distribution Failure Case
A pale pink yarn was considered as an out-of-distribution case, since it was not included in training, validation or test sets. In this condition, more than 32% of samples were misclassified and the (H_0) and (H_1) LLR distributions overlapped substantially.
This result indicates that extremely low-contrast yarn/background combinations lie outside the current operating domain and require more robust or learned features.

title: Results and Efficiency
text:
Real-Time Operation on Raspberry Pi 3
The complete acquisition and detection pipeline runs directly on the Raspberry Pi 3 and is triggered by the synchronization event. During the error-recognition experiments, the event interval was approximately (0.42,), corresponding to an inspection rate of:
\[
f_{\text{inspect}} \approx 2.4 \ \text{inspections/s}
\]
At each trigger, a full-resolution image is captured, cropped to a (76 ) region of interest and processed through preprocessing, normalized cross-correlation scoring and LLR evaluation.
The processing time remains below the interval between consecutive synchronization events. The available computational margin also enables future multi-frame decision fusion strategies, such as majority voting or LLR averaging.

4.4 Enable Raspberry Pi Interfaces
The GFX HAT requires the Raspberry Pi hardware interfaces.
Open the configuration menu:
sudo raspi-config
Enable:
Interface Options → I2C → Enable
Interface Options → SPI → Enable
Then reboot the Raspberry Pi:
sudo reboot


4.5 Give Serial Permission to the User
To allow the Raspberry Pi user to access the ESP32 through USB serial, add the user to the dialout group:
sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER
Then reboot:
sudo reboot

5. Insert the USB Drive into the Machine
After creating the PNG on the user computer, insert the USB flash drive into the machine.
The Raspberry Pi inside the machine will read the PNG files from the USB drive.

title: Operating the Machine
section: 6. Mount the USB Drive on the Raspberry Pi
text:
6. Mount the USB Drive on the Raspberry Pi
Check the device name assigned to the USB drive:
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,LABEL,MOUNTPOINTS
In the current prototype, the USB drive is usually detected as:
/dev/sda1
Create the mount folder if it does not already exist:
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/pattern_usb
Mount the USB drive:
sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/pattern_usb
Check that the PNG files are visible:
ls /mnt/pattern_usb
If the USB drive has a different device name, replace /dev/sda1 with the correct one.

title: Operating the Machine
Operating the Machine
text:
8. Find the ESP32 Serial Port
Check which serial port is assigned to the ESP32:
ls /dev/ttyUSB*
or:
ls /dev/ttyACM*
In the current prototype, the ESP32 is usually available as:
/dev/ttyUSB0
If the ESP32 appears with a different name, use that port when running the application.

title: Operating the Machine
text:
9. Start the Raspberry Pi Application
Activate the virtual environment:
source /home/aless/venvs/uncinetto/bin/activate
Run the integrated interface:
python3 /home/aless/gfxhat_pattern_ui_usb.py --usb-dir /mnt/pattern_usb --port /dev/ttyUSB0
If the ESP32 is detected as /dev/ttyACM0, use:
python3 /home/aless/gfxhat_pattern_ui_usb.py --usb-dir /mnt/pattern_usb --port /dev/ttyACM0
The command starts the Raspberry Pi interface, reads the PNG files from the USB drive and opens the serial communication with the ESP32.

text:
16. Unmount the USB Drive
Before removing the USB flash drive from the machine, unmount it safely:
sudo umount /mnt/pattern_usb
The USB drive can then be physically removed from the Raspberry Pi.
